# Abstract

This study reconstructs the pre-Columbian and early contact population of the Southeast Hydrological Unit (USGS HU 03, extending across adjacent Gulf and Tennessee margin watersheds) over 682.076 km² (9.721 five-arcminute cells) from 10000BC to 1600AD. Linking radiocarbon summed probability distributions (N = 1.716, median peak 1169AD) [@kelly2025] with Archaic shell-ring geoarchaeology [@cannarozzi2019seasonal; @garland2022multi], Mississippian mound excavations [@anderson1994; @knight1998; @king2003], Savannah valley emigration syntheses [@ritchison2018; @ritchison2022] and early Spanish and English expedition records [@hudson1997; @milanich1995], the region partitions into four watershed divisions encompassing 115 catalogued settlements across 220 ledger candidates (after 105 duplicate-alias consolidations).

Total numbers rise slowly from 3.150 (bounds 2.898-3.402) in 10000BC to 234k (215,3k-252,7k) by 2000BC and 411k (378,1k-443,9k) at 0AD as coastal shell-mound fisheries and Piedmont riverine horticulture deepen carrying capacity. Woodland ceremonial mound building and Mississippian maize intensification lift the basin to 684k in 1000AD and a Holocene peak of 707k (650,4k-763,6k; 1,04 persons per km²) in 1200AD.

Fourteenth-century droughts, palisaded warfare and middle Savannah abandonment reduce numbers by 17,1% to 586k in 1400AD before late Mississippian provinces rebuild totals to 614k (564,9k-663,1k) at 1500AD. Sustained Spanish contact, inland expeditions and introduced Old World pathogens then cut the regional population by 45,3% across the sixteenth century to 336k (309,1k-362,9k) in 1600AD [@milner2010; @jones2014].

# Background

USGS HU 03 sweeps from the Roanoke, Yadkin-Pee Dee and Santee-Wateree river valleys of Virginia and the Carolinas through the Savannah, Ocmulgee and Coosa-Etowah basins of Georgia, across the Black Warrior, Alabama and Tombigbee-Mobile drainages, and south into the Apalachicola valley and Peninsular Florida. Across nearly seven hundred thousand square kilometres of Piedmont red-clay valleys, Fall Line shoals, broad Coastal Plain pinewoods and subtropical limestone peninsulas, long frost-free growing seasons and prolific coastal estuaries sustained the densest Indigenous population in eastern North America prior to European arrival [@milner2010; @ubelaker2006].

The demographic history of this Atlantic and Eastern Gulf province turns on two structural contrasts: the gulf between fertile riverine bottoms and sandy interfluvial pine barrens, and the tension between maritime littoral stability and interior chiefdom cycling. Along the Atlantic coast from South Carolina to northeast Florida and along the southwestern Calusa shelf, estuarine oysters, schooling fish and wetland tubers supported dense sedentary or semi-sedentary communities millennia before maize agriculture arrived [@cannarozzi2019seasonal; @thompson2016shell].

By contrast, interior population growth accelerated sharply whenever communities mastered floodplain cultivation along the Black Warrior, Etowah, Ocmulgee and Wateree terraces. Yet those same alluvial centres proved sensitive to multi-year droughts and riverine political collapse, creating cycles of nucleation and abandonment across Piedmont and Coastal Plain watersheds [@anderson1994; @ritchison2018].

Using 1.716 cleaned radiocarbon dates across HU 03, Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] place the basin's median summed probability peak at 1169AD, roughly half a century after Cahokia's apex in the Upper Mississippi and a century earlier than East Texas Caddoan polities. That twelfth-century peak corresponds on the ground to the first great platform-mound florescence at Okmulgi, Etowah and Moundville [@knight1998; @king2003].

Archaeological chronologies nevertheless show sharp divergence after 1350AD. Severe droughts in 1360AD-1377AD preceded the wholesale abandonment of the middle Savannah River valley around 1450AD and shifted people toward the Georgia coast, the Appalachian margins and the upper Alabama-Coosa valleys [@anderson1994; @ritchison2018; @ritchison2022].

Long before the first European ships sighted Florida in 1513AD, southeastern coastal margins had already absorbed substantial Holocene shoreline change. Regional heritage inventories and coastal vulnerability models demonstrate how sea-level rise and storm surges submerge or erode low-lying shell rings and tidal villages [@anderson2017level; @howland2024modeling]. Early twentieth-century drainage works and coastal dredging also altered estuarine habitats and obscured baseline distributions of key fauna such as the Florida manatee [@pluckhahn2024historical], so demographic reconstruction must balance monumental interior centres against drowned or eroded littoral middens.

# Methodology

## Radiocarbon Kriging and Sub-Regional Partitioning

Rural spatial priors at five-arcminute resolution come from the continental North American radiocarbon compilation, which merges global syntheses (p3k14c [@bird2022p3k14c] and c14bazAAR) with state site files and regional archaeological inventories [@kelly2022; @crema2021]. After spatial and chronological deduplication across 200-year bins over 493.687 continental land cells (18.561.382 km², with 129.716 to 133.990 active inhabited cells per horizon), the North American domain holds 92.500 unique site-period observations (166.545 horizon site records) grouped across 3.832 domestic Voronoi catchments spanning 15,52M km² (2.562 active inhabited catchments covering 66,86% of the domain, equivalent circular radius median 29,48 km and 90th-percentile radius 41 km overall, or 29,31 km median and 39,86 km 90th-percentile across active catchments), representing a 14,15x increase in site density over the 6.539-entry legacy global radiocarbon baseline.

Across ten Holocene horizons from 13000BC to 1650AD, 2D Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging pairs Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation with biophysical covariates for coastal proximity, fluvial distance decay and terrain slope. Along the southeastern maritime perimeter, 251 continental cross-frontier buffer catchments condition Cuba and the Bahamas across the Straits of Florida so island edges never depress southern Florida coastal weights.

Within HU 03, 9.721 active five-arcminute land pixels (682.076 km²) partition into four contiguous sub-regional masks (Table \ref{tab:se-subregion-profiles}):

1. **Roanoke, Yadkin-Pee Dee and Santee-Wateree** (203.010 km², 2.999 cells, 25 catalogued sites): spans the Virginia-North Carolina Fall Line, the Carolina Piedmont and the coastal plain south to the Savannah watershed divide, anchoring Cactus Hill, Fig Island, Town Creek, Joara, Mulberry and Cofitachequi.
2. **Georgia Savannah, Ocmulgee and Chattahoochee Basins** (149.441 km², 2.106 cells, 29 catalogued sites): covers the Savannah, Altamaha-Ocmulgee and Flint-Chattahoochee watersheds, containing Topper, Stallings Island, Kolomoki, Okmulgi, Irene Mound, Rood's Landing, Singer-Moye and Lamar.
3. **Alabama, Black Warrior, Coosa and Tombigbee-Mobile Basins** (196.353 km², 2.741 cells, 28 catalogued sites): encompasses the Coosa-Etowah, Tallapoosa, Black Warrior, Tombigbee, Alabama and Pensacola-Mobile drainages, centred on Etowah, Moundville, Coosa, Bottle Creek, Mabila, Lubbub Creek and Tukabatchee.
4. **Peninsular Florida and Apalachicola** (133.272 km², 1.875 cells, 33 catalogued sites): covers the Apalachicola-Flint confluence, St. Johns valley, Tampa Bay, Lake Okeechobee and Calusa southwest coast, anchoring Page-Ladson, Windover, Crystal River, Anhaica, Lake Jackson Mounds, San Luis de Talimali and Mound Key.

## Subsistence Calibration, Chronology and Uncertainty Bounds

Sub-regional totals across 23 chronological horizons from 10000BC to 1600AD weigh floodplain maize-beans-squash carrying capacities against Archaic and Woodland foraging yields. In prime Mississippian river valleys such as the Black Warrior, Wateree and Etowah, localised alluvial corridors supported 2 to 4,5 persons per km², yet broad stretches of interfluvial Coastal Plain pine flats and karst scrub held sparser dispersed hamlets, keeping overall sub-regional mean densities near 0,9 to 1,24 persons per km² at the 1200AD peak [@milner2010; @knight1998; @king2003].

Along the Atlantic barrier islands and southwest Florida estuaries, permanent shell-ring and midden-mound towns compensated for thin sandy soils through year-round shellfish, mullet and estuarine turtle harvesting [@cannarozzi2019seasonal; @thompson2016shell; @milanich1995]. Point-settlement populations for all 115 catalogued sites are subtracted from each sub-regional total prior to allocating residual rural population across the five-arcminute kriged surface, followed by two 5-pixel smoothing passes to eliminate sharp mask seams along watershed boundaries.

Symmetric uncertainty bounds of plus or minus 8 per cent around each sub-regional estimate capture archaeological uncertainties in household floor-area ratios, contemporary village spacing, marine reservoir offsets in coastal radiocarbon series and epidemiological mortality rates during the sixteenth century [@jones2014; @ubelaker2006; @garland2022multi]. Comparative multi-proxy and isotopic studies from outside the basin (covering spatial heterogeneity in shell-midden accumulation [@hausmann2019quantifying], shellmound stratigraphy [@cardoso2024late], Holocene sea-level highstand redating [@dougherty2019redating] and dietary social differentiation [@sharpe2025isotopic]) inform our calibration of taphonomic bias and elite-commoner settlement footprints without altering local southeastern carrying capacities.

# Testing and Validation

All spatial, variogram, gazetteer and arithmetic checks clear pre-publication thresholds at GMT+0:

1. **Kriging Sharpness and Fit**: Across all ten Holocene horizons (13000BC to 1650AD) over 493.687 North American active cells (129.716 to 133.990 active inhabited cells per horizon), the non-stationary Matérn variograms achieve regularised dimensionless scale $\tau_1 = 1,35$ across all ten horizons (raw $\tau_1$ spanning 1,4834 to 1,6067, mean 1,5861), range scale $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), effective short range 44,17 km to 47,85 km (mean 47,23 km), raw nugget-to-sill ratio 0 across all ten horizons, regularised nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04 across all ten horizons and weighted least-squares residual $R^2$ from 0,9991 to 0,9993 (Table \ref{tab:se-kriging-horizons}).
2. **Gazetteer Balance and Containment**: Of 220 evaluated candidates in the regional ledger, 115 discrete settlements enter the active point gazetteer (25 in Carolina Piedmont-Santee, 29 in Georgia Basins, 28 in Alabama-Tombigbee and 33 in Florida-Apalachicola) and 105 duplicate coordinate and alias records within 2 km are consolidated into canonical entries, leaving 0 unaccounted records and 0 non-alias exclusions.
3. **Arithmetic Continuity**: Across all 23 benchmark horizons from 10000BC (3.150) to 1600AD (336k), the four sub-regional series sum exactly to the regional headline totals reported in Table \ref{tab:se-benchmarks} and match the 682.076 km² areal mask cell by cell.

# Results

## Palaeoindian Springs and Archaic Shell Rings (10000BC to 1000BC)

At the terminal Pleistocene transition in 10000BC, lower sea levels exposed wide coastal shelves along the Carolinas, Georgia and Florida while cooler, drier interior forests concentrated human bands around reliable springs, chert outcrops and major river terraces. Total basin population stood near 3.150 (2.898-3.402), anchored by early occupations at Cactus Hill on the Nottoway River (45 in 10000BC), Topper along the middle Savannah (25) and submerged karst sinkholes such as Page-Ladson (25), Little Salt Spring and Warm Mineral Springs in Florida. By 8000BC, post-glacial warming and oak-hickory expansion lifted regional numbers to 13,4k, quadrupling over two millennia as foraging groups expanded across the Hardaway Piedmont and Florida Gulf karst.

Between 7000BC and 3000BC, population multiplied more than sixfold from 25,6k to 168,5k as Early and Middle Archaic bands established persistent seasonal cemeteries and riverine shell heaps. Wetland peat burials at Windover (80-120 between 6200BC and 5200BC) on the Atlantic coastal ridge and shell-mound accumulations along the St. Johns valley at Tick Island (90-180) and Silver Glen (85-210) document dense aquatic exploitation even before ceramic vessels existed.

By 2000BC, total population reached 234k (0,34 persons per km²), marked by Late Archaic fibre-tempered pottery and circular shell-ring villages along the Savannah-Georgia littoral: Stallings Island (260 at 2000BC), Fig Island (280 at 1900BC), Sapelo Shell Ring (310 at 1500BC), St. Catherines Ring (260 at 1800BC) and Horr's Island on the southwest Florida coast (4500BC onward). Isotopic and sclerochronological analyses of Georgia shell rings demonstrate multi-season oyster harvesting and local environmental responses to mid-to-late Holocene sea-level fluctuations between 2500BC and 1800BC [@cannarozzi2019seasonal; @garland2022multi; @anderson2017level]. By 1000BC, basin numbers climbed to 315k, roughly balanced across Carolina (86k, 27,3%), Georgia (81k, 25,7%), Alabama (77k, 24,4%) and Florida (71k, 22,5%).

## Woodland Ceremonial Centres and Coastal Chiefdoms (1000BC to 900AD)

During the Woodland millennium from 1000BC to 0AD, steady growth in native seed horticulture (goosefoot, sumpweed and sunflower), pottery exchange and coastal fisheries carried HU 03 from 315k to 411k (bounds 378,1k-443,9k). The pace of growth eased slightly compared with the Archaic, climbing 14,6% between 0AD and 200AD (to 471k) and another 25,7% over the next four centuries to 592k in 600AD.

Middle Woodland mound and earthwork centres knit wide interior and coastal networks together across both Gulf and Piedmont corridors. Crystal River (620 at 200AD) and Letchworth Mounds (560 at 400AD) anchored Florida's Gulf edge, Leake (520 at 200AD) flourished in the Etowah valley, and the Kolomoki plaza complex in southwestern Georgia reached 1,65k at 600AD, flanked by coastal shell settlements at Pineland (580 at 600AD) and Bayshore Homes (520 at 700AD).

Late Woodland population growth slowed further between 600AD and 800AD, rising 9,3% to 647k (178k in Carolina, 169k in Georgia, 160k in Alabama and 140k in Florida). Across this two-century interval, coastal groups in south and central Florida intensified anthropogenic island construction at Mound Key (480 by 800AD) [@thompson2016shell] and Pineland, whereas interior Piedmont and Coastal Plain villagers faced localized subsistence stress during bow-and-arrow adoption before intensive tropical maize took hold.

## Mississippian Florescence and Regional Divergence (900AD to 1400AD)

Between 900AD and 1200AD, intensive maize agriculture, floodplain hoe cultivation and platform-mound ceremonialism lifted the Southeast to its pre-contact zenith (Figure \ref{fig:se-trajectory}). Basin population rose from 647k in 800AD to 684k in 1000AD, 700k in 1100AD and a maximum of 707k (bounds 650,4k-763,6k) in 1200AD, closely shadowing Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] 1169AD radiocarbon summed probability peak. At 1200AD, population was spread remarkably evenly across all four sub-regions: Carolina Piedmont-Santee held 196k (27,7% share; 0,97 persons per km²), Georgia Savannah-Ocmulgee held 186k (26,3%; 1,24 persons per km²), Alabama-Tombigbee held 176k (24,9%; 0,9 persons per km²) and Peninsular Florida-Apalachicola held 149k (21,1%; 1,12 persons per km²).

Urban nucleation concentrated at riverine junctions linking Piedmont shoals to Coastal Plain floodplains. Okmulgi on the Macon Plateau peaked early at 2,1k around 1100AD, before Etowah in the Coosa-Etowah corridor (3,5k in 1200AD; 4,2k in 1300AD) [@king2003] and Moundville along the Black Warrior (2,8k in 1200AD; 3,5k in 1300AD) [@knight1998] became the largest towns south of the Ohio. Secondary temple-mound capitals multiplied across every drainage: Irene Mound (1,15k at 1300AD) near the mouth of the Savannah, Rood's Landing (860) and Singer-Moye (780) on the lower Chattahoochee, Town Creek (820) on the Little Pee Dee, Lubbub Creek (580) and Bessemer Mounds (560) in Alabama, and Fort Walton (560), Safety Harbor (780), Madira Bickel Mound (540) and Mount Royal (540) across Florida.

After 1250AD, Mississippian chiefdom stability fractured. Palisaded ditches and skeletal trauma frequencies rose across eastern North America [@milner2013; @krus2016], while prolonged droughts in 1360AD-1377AD disrupted maize harvests along the Savannah corridor [@anderson1994]. Aggregate HU 03 numbers fell 8,9% between 1200AD and 1300AD (to 644k) and dropped a further 9% to 586k (bounds 539,1k-632,9k) by 1400AD, marking a cumulative 17,1% contraction from the 1200AD peak.

Georgia (186k down to 145k, -22%) and Alabama (176k down to 138k, -21,6%) absorbed the sharpest interior losses as Moundville shed outlying residential wards and middle Savannah mound centres including Lawton, Hollywood and eventually Irene Mound were evacuated [@anderson1994; @knight1998; @ritchison2018; @ritchison2022]. Florida proved far more resilient, dipping only 9,4% from 149k to 135k between 1200AD and 1400AD because maritime estuarine resources at Pineland (920 at 1200AD), Mound Key (1,6k at 1400AD) and Bottle Creek (1,4k at 1400AD on the Mobile-Tensaw delta) buffered against interior crop failure [@thompson2016shell; @milanich1995].

## Late Pre-Contact Provinces and Sixteenth-Century Collapse (1400AD to 1600AD)

During the fifteenth century, surviving chiefdoms coalesced into larger regional confederacies and provinces, lifting HU 03 back by 4,8% to 614k (564,9k-663,1k) in 1500AD (Figure \ref{fig:se-shares}). In South Carolina, Cofitachequi (1,45k at 1500AD) and neighbouring Mulberry (1,8k) anchored the Wateree chiefdom; in upper Georgia and eastern Tennessee borderlands, Coosa (1,8k in 1500AD; 2,2k in 1550AD) knit together towns including King Site (580), Nacoochee (620) and Tugalo (520); along the central Georgia Fall Line, Lamar (880), Shoulderbone Mounds (680) and Scull Shoals (540) replaced older Macon Plateau sites.

To the south and west, Lake Jackson Mounds (1,6k at 1500AD) and Anhaica (1,2k at 1539AD) anchored the Apalachee province [@milanich1995], while Mabila (1,5k in 1500AD; 2,2k at 1540AD) dominated central Alabama. Along the southwest Florida coast, the Calusa capital at Mound Key expanded through engineered shell-midden terraces and canals to 2,1k in 1500AD and 2,4k in 1550AD [@thompson2016shell]. Across all four divisions in 1500AD, Carolina held 176k (28,7%), Georgia 152k (24,8%), Alabama 144k (23,5%) and Florida 142k (23,1%).

European contact after 1513AD precipitated severe demographic contraction [@hudson1997; @milanich1995; @jones2014]. Opening with Ponce de León, Ayllón's 1526AD Carolina coast colony and Narváez's 1528AD Florida landing, European incursions continued with Hernando de Soto's 1539AD-1541AD march across Apalachee, Cofitachequi, Coosa and Mabila, Luna's 1559AD-1561AD Pensacola expedition, Juan Pardo's 1566AD-1568AD Piedmont campaigns to Joara (920 at 1550AD), and the founding of Fort Caroline (300 in 1564AD), St. Augustine (1565AD) and Roanoke Island (117 in 1587AD). Regional numbers plunged 24,4% in half a century to 464k in 1550AD and fell to 336k (309,1k-362,9k) in 1600AD, an overall 45,3% loss since 1500AD and 52,5% below the 1200AD Holocene peak.

Losses varied markedly by corridor (Table \ref{tab:se-subregions}). Peninsular Florida and Apalachicola dropped 52,1% from 142k in 1500AD to 68k in 1600AD as coastal slaving, Spanish missionisation around St. Augustine and San Luis de Talimali (1,1k at 1600AD) and epidemic waves eroded Timucua and coastal provinces even while Calusa Mound Key remained strongly populated (1,8k in 1600AD). Alabama-Tombigbee dropped 47,2% from 144k to 76k following the destruction of Mabila in 1540AD and subsequent Creek-Choctaw reorganisation around Tukabatchee (1,2k at 1600AD) and Taskigi.

Georgia fell 44,7% from 152k to 84k as coastal Guale missions replaced earlier Mississippian towns, while the Carolina Piedmont and Virginia borderlands declined more moderately by 38,6% from 176k to 108k. That slower upland attrition lifted Carolina's relative share of HU 03 to 32,1% in 1600AD, buffered by interior Piedmont refugia around Joara, Upper Saratown (520), Graham-White (420) and Tidewater Quiyoughcohannock (580) [@ubelaker2006; @milner2010; @jones2014].

## Sub-Regional Demographic Balances and Urban Hierarchy

Comparing the four hydrological divisions across eleven millennia reveals distinct regional rhythms masked by basin-wide totals (Table \ref{tab:se-subregions} and Table \ref{tab:se-leading-centres}). The Roanoke-Santee-Carolina division (203.010 km²) began modestly at 900 inhabitants in 10000BC and grew steadily to 196k in 1200AD, sustaining the highest territorial share throughout prehistory and widening that lead during the sixteenth-century upland buffer. Its urban hierarchy remained dispersed rather than monocentric, led by Mulberry (1,8k), Cofitachequi (1,45k), Joara (920), Town Creek (820) and Adamson (680) across Piedmont terraces and Fall Line rapids [@anderson1994].

Georgia's Savannah, Ocmulgee and Chattahoochee basins (149.441 km²) displayed the sharpest boom-and-bust amplitude of any southeastern division. Rising from 800 inhabitants in 10000BC to 186k in 1200AD (1,24 persons per km², the basin's highest sub-regional density), it supported both the Middle Woodland ceremonial monument at Kolomoki (1,65k) and Mississippian platform-mound towns at Okmulgi (2,1k at 1100AD) and Irene Mound (1,15k at 1300AD), before Savannah valley abandonment and post-contact epidemics reduced totals to 84k by 1600AD [@anderson1994; @ritchison2022].

The Black Warrior, Alabama, Coosa and Tombigbee-Mobile corridor (196.353 km²) sustained lower average density (0,9 persons per km² at 1200AD; 176k) across its broader interior drainage, yet anchored the region's largest monumental polities at Etowah (4,2k at 1300AD) [@king2003] and Moundville (3,5k at 1300AD) [@knight1998], deltaic Bottle Creek (1,4k at 1400AD), contact-era Coosa (2,2k at 1550AD) and Mabila (2,2k at 1540AD), and protohistoric Creek centres at Tukabatchee (1,2k at 1600AD). By contrast, Peninsular Florida and the Apalachicola basin (133.272 km²) held 33 of the region's 115 catalogued sites (28,7%) within the most compact watershed division (1,12 persons per km² at 1200AD), reflecting high coastal archaeological visibility and dense maritime shell-midden towns from Pineland and Crystal River to Apalachee Lake Jackson Mounds (1,6k) and Calusa Mound Key (2,4k), even as its post-1500AD share tumbled most precipitously under Spanish coastal contact [@milanich1995; @thompson2016shell].

# Limitations

Four structural constraints qualify the southeastern reconstruction. First, Holocene sea-level rise and coastal erosion along the Atlantic Sea Islands and Gulf barrier shores submerge or destroy Archaic and early Woodland settlements, particularly before 2500BC [@anderson2017level; @howland2024modeling; @dougherty2019redating]. Because radiocarbon databases filter out shell dates carrying variable marine reservoir corrections [@kelly2025], estuarine density priors risk under-weighting southwest Florida and Georgia coast middens relative to interior Piedmont valleys [@milanich1995; @cannarozzi2019seasonal].

Second, survey intensity varies strongly across modern land-use regimes. Highway and reservoir salvage surveys inflate site counts around urbanising Piedmont corridors and river impoundments, whereas longleaf pine plantations and Okefenokee or Everglades wetlands remain comparatively under-sampled; Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation and 2.562 active North American catchments damp this distortion but cannot remove it altogether.

Third, historical chroniclers of the De Soto, Luna and Pardo expeditions observed principal towns selectively along major river corridors while bypassing dispersed pinewoods hamlets. Post-contact mortality interpolation between 1540AD and 1600AD therefore depends heavily on regional archaeological phase contractions where written Spanish mission rolls are sparse outside coastal Florida and Guale [@hudson1997; @milner2010; @jones2014].

Fourth, watershed boundaries along the upper Coosa, Etowah and Blue Ridge divide bisect chiefdom territories shared between HU 03 and HU 06 (Cumberland and Tennessee). Although the continental radiocarbon compilation and cross-watershed smoothing eliminate artificial numerical cliffs across the spatial grid, macro-regional urban inventories must deduplicate borderland centres so shared polities are never double-counted.

# Conclusion

Across 11,6 millennia from 10000BC to 1600AD, the Southeast Hydrological Unit supported a sustained expansion from 3.150 Palaeoindian foragers to a Holocene maximum of 707k inhabitants in 1200AD, before climatic stress, political fragmentation and Old World diseases halved numbers to 336k by 1600AD.

Rather than progressing through a single uniform trajectory, regional demography combined deep coastal estuarine stability (rooted in Late Archaic shell rings and enduring through Calusa Mound Key) with sharper cycles of alluvial maize intensification and chiefdom rise and collapse across the Piedmont and Gulf plains. Coupling 115 catalogued sites with the 92.500-observation North American kriging surface preserves both the demographic weight of major platform-mound capitals and the wide rural hinterland that sustained them into the colonial transition.
